# Discussion {#sec:discussion}

## Workloads the measurements support

The evaluation separates two kinds of pipeline, and the case for vectra
differs between them.

For **streaming pipelines**, which filter, derive, and select and then write
to a file or fold the batches in R, vectra's peak memory stays near one batch
regardless of input size. It was the lowest of the four tools on the collect
and sink workloads, and it did not rise with input size (Section
\@ref(sec:eval)). These are the pipelines that convert, clean, and subset
large sources before any modelling. They also connect to R most directly,
through `collect_chunked()` and `chunk_feeder()`, without an intermediate
copy of the result.

For **stateful relational work**, which groups, joins, and sorts,
vectra completes these workloads within a configurable budget and spills
beyond it. On this machine it was, however, consistently slower than DuckDB
and arrow, and at its default budget it used more memory than both
(Section \@ref(sec:eval)). The main cause is a design decision: every grouped
aggregation passes through an external sort. That bounds memory
independently of the number of groups, but it makes aggregation over a few
groups cost as much as a sort of the aggregated columns. Where a pipeline is
dominated by large aggregations or joins and needs to run many times, DuckDB
is the faster engine. Where the table fits in memory, data.table remains
the simplest fast option.

The case for vectra is therefore not raw relational speed. It is a single
engine, installed as an ordinary R package, that covers the whole path from
a source file too large for R, through grouping, joins, and point-in-polygon
operations on the same stream, to a model fitted by R code on batches or
partitions, with a memory account for every step. The spatial benchmark is
where this composition pays most directly. vectra tagged points with
countries faster than DuckDB's spatial extension and with a fraction of the
memory \pkg{sf} needed, and sf could not complete the largest point sets at
all.

## Semantic limits

vectra implements dplyr-like verbs but is not a dplyr backend. Its generics
mask dplyr's when both are attached, it covers a subset of the verbs, and
it rejects expressions it cannot translate to its C evaluator rather than
falling back to R. A few verbs (`slice_tail()`, `reframe()`, `slice_min()`
with ties) do collect their input into R, and they are documented as doing
so. Output order after grouping and joins is not guaranteed, as in SQL. A
plan is consumed when it runs, which differs from arrow's and dbplyr's
re-executable queries, and is the reason `offload()` and plan factories
exist.

The optimiser is deliberately small. Predicate pushdown applies only to a
filter placed directly above a `.vtr` scan, and column pruning stops at the
first `mutate()`. The ablation in Section \@ref(sec:eval) shows that these
limits change the cost of equivalent queries by more than an order of
magnitude, so the order in which a user writes the verbs matters more than it
does in engines with a cost-based optimiser. Pushing predicates through
projections, and pruning through `mutate()`, are the next improvements to
make.

## Resource limits

The memory budget bounds each subsystem's estimate of its own buffered
state. It is not a hard limit on the process. The measured peak of a grouped
aggregation at the default budget exceeded the budget by the sorting working
space, and a plan with several stateful nodes may hold several budgets at
once. The spatial and partition verbs buffer their output as R data frames
before spilling, so part of their memory is R's representation rather than
the engine's. Partition routing in `offload(by =)` runs in R and writes one
run file per key and flush, which becomes expensive for keys with many
thousands of values. `method = "hash"` bounds the number of shards in that
case. Spilling costs disk space as well as time: an external sort writes its
input once more, and a spatial join on coordinate columns writes a WKB
geometry column for every output row.

## Storage and dependency choices

The `.vtr` format is specific to vectra. It gives the engine per-row-group
statistics, dictionary-aware string decoding, in-place appends, fingerprinted
indexes, and quantised or spatially predicted numeric columns, and it lets
the package be built without any external compression library. The cost is
interoperability. Other tools cannot read `.vtr`, and vectra does not read
Parquet or Arrow IPC, the formats in which much large ecological data is now
distributed, including the GBIF snapshots used in Section \@ref(sec:case). In
the case study, arrow read the Parquet files and vectra appended them to a
`.vtr` store. The GeoTIFF reader decodes uncompressed and DEFLATE-compressed
files but not LZW, the compression WorldClim distributes, so the climate
layers were re-encoded once with \pkg{terra}. A Parquet reader, and LZW
decoding for GeoTIFF, would remove both conversion steps.

"No external dependencies" would overstate the package's position.
vectra's C code depends only on the C standard library and on sources it
vendors, the \pkg{tdc} codec and the miniz deflate library. The readers and
writers for CSV, SQLite database files, and GeoTIFF are vectra's own code. At the R level, however, the package imports
\CRANpkg{tidyselect}, \CRANpkg{rlang}, \CRANpkg{libgeos}, and \pkg{parallel},
and it links to \CRANpkg{libgeos} for the GEOS C API. \CRANpkg{libgeos}
bundles GEOS, so no system library is needed, but it is a compiled
dependency of about 3 MB. The spatial verbs additionally require \pkg{sf},
and with it GDAL and PROJ, although the geometry computations themselves run
on the GEOS API without going through sf. The practical consequence is that
the tabular engine compiles wherever R and a C11 compiler are available,
while the spatial layer inherits sf's installation requirements.

## Summary

vectra lets an R user carry an analysis on data larger than memory from the
source file to a fitted model within one package. It states, for each
operation, which quantity of the data sets its memory. The measurements show
streaming work at near-constant memory, stateful work bounded by a
configurable budget at a clear cost in time relative to DuckDB, and
streaming spatial joins that remain practical at sizes where in-memory
spatial tools fail. The case study shows the pieces composing into a
reproducible macroecological analysis of 401 million records on a machine
with 8 GB of memory.
